entity.name: Nostradamus
entity.description: The plague doctor who became history's most famous prophet. Nostradamus published 942 cryptic quatrains in Les Propheties that people have been arguing about for five centuries. He was also an apothecary expelled from medical school, a widower who lost his first family to plague, and personal astrologer to Catherine de' Medici.

story.name: Nostradamus
story.description: Expelled from medical school, loses his family to plague, publishes 942 cryptic prophecies, becomes astrologer to the Queen of France, and allegedly predicts his own death. The original doomsday prophet.

moments.name: Nostradamus Is Born to a Recently Converted Jewish Family in Provence
moments.subtitle: His grandfather converted from Judaism just one generation earlier, taking the name Notre Dame
moments.description: In December 1503, Michel de Nostredame is born in Saint-Remy-de-Provence, France, one of at least nine children of the notary Jaume de Nostredame. The family had converted from Judaism to Catholicism just one generation prior—Nostradamus's grandfather Cresquas, a grain dealer in Avignon, took the Christian surname Nostredame (Our Lady) around 1459-60 on the saint's day of his conversion. This recently converted status in an era of Inquisitorial suspicion will shadow Nostradamus throughout his life, contributing to his later conflicts with Church authorities. His birthplace in Saint-Remy still stands today.

moments.name: Nostradamus Is Expelled from Medical School for Working as an Apothecary
moments.subtitle: The expulsion document still sits in the university library nearly 500 years later
moments.description: In 1529, Nostradamus enters the University of Montpellier to study for a doctorate in medicine. He is expelled almost immediately when the student procurator Guillaume Rondelet discovers that Nostradamus had previously worked as an apothecary—a manual trade expressly forbidden by university statutes—and had been slandering doctors. The expulsion document (Register S 2 folio 87) still exists in the Montpellier faculty library. Despite never earning his doctorate, some publishers and correspondents will later call him Doctor. The rejection from institutional medicine helps push Nostradamus toward the occult career that will make him famous.

moments.name: Nostradamus Loses His Wife and Two Children to the Plague in Agen
moments.subtitle: The man who treated plague victims cannot save his own family
moments.description: In 1534, Nostradamus's first wife and their two children die in Agen, presumably from the plague. Nostradamus had come to Agen in 1531 at the invitation of the Renaissance scholar Jules-Cesar Scaliger, married there, and started a family. The devastating loss—a plague doctor unable to protect his own household—drives Nostradamus back onto the road. He travels through France and possibly Italy for over a decade before eventually settling in Salon-de-Provence in 1547 and remarrying. The personal catastrophe transforms Nostradamus from a conventional apothecary-healer into the restless, spiritually searching figure who will turn to prophecy.

moments.name: Nostradamus Publishes 353 Cryptic Quatrains Predicting the Future
moments.subtitle: Written in scrambled syntax mixing French, Latin, Greek, and Provencal to dodge heresy charges
moments.description: In 1555, Nostradamus publishes the first edition of Les Propheties from his home in Salon-de-Provence, containing 353 poetic quatrains claiming to predict future events. Fearing persecution, Nostradamus obscures his meaning using scrambled Virgilian syntax, word games, and a mixture of French, Greek, Italian, Latin, and Provencal. The book receives a mixed reception—some call Nostradamus a servant of evil, while elites take him seriously. Catherine de' Medici, wife of King Henry II, reads his almanacs and summons him to Paris. The book will eventually contain 942 quatrains and become the most famous collection of prophecies ever published.

moments.name: Catherine de' Medici Summons Nostradamus to Paris to Read the Royal Future
moments.subtitle: The prophet fears beheading but instead becomes royal astrologer to the French crown
moments.description: In 1555, after reading Nostradamus's almanacs hinting at unnamed threats to the royal family, Catherine de' Medici—wife of King Henry II of France—summons the prophet to Paris to explain his predictions and draw horoscopes for her children. Nostradamus reportedly fears he will be beheaded. Instead, the queen becomes his greatest patron. By the time of his death in 1566, Catherine has appointed Nostradamus Counselor and Physician-in-Ordinary to her son, the young King Charles IX. The royal endorsement transforms a provincial astrologer into the most famous seer in European history.

moments.name: Nostradamus Tells His Secretary He Will Not Survive the Night—and Doesn't
moments.subtitle: Found dead on the floor the next morning, exactly as he allegedly predicted
moments.description: On the evening of July 1, 1566, Nostradamus—suffering from gout that has developed into edema—allegedly tells his secretary Jean de Chavigny that he will not be found alive at sunrise. The next morning, Nostradamus is reportedly found dead on the floor beside his bed in Salon-de-Provence at roughly age sixty-two. Days earlier, he had summoned his lawyer to draw up a will bequeathing property and 3,444 crowns (roughly $300,000 today) to his wife and children. Nostradamus is buried in the local Franciscan chapel in Salon, later re-interred during the French Revolution at the Collegiale Saint-Laurent, where his tomb remains today.
